claims.text: Brittle behavior in initially single-phase high-entropy alloys is primarily governed by intrinsic grain-boundary morphology.
Straight grain boundaries cause greater localized strain concentration than serrated grain boundaries.
Localized strain at straight grain boundaries promotes intergranular decohesion.
Intergranular decohesion associated with straight grain boundaries leads to toughness degradation.
Serrated grain boundaries distribute strain more uniformly than straight grain boundaries.
More uniform strain distribution at serrated grain boundaries helps maintain ductility.
Controlled heat treatments can produce predominantly serrated and predominantly straight grain-boundary morphologies in otherwise identical samples.
Optimized cooling rates can produce serrated grain boundaries.
The serrated-boundary baseline has better-distributed strain and enhanced toughness.
Samples with straight grain boundaries will have lower fracture toughness than samples with serrated grain boundaries.
Samples with straight grain boundaries will exhibit a more brittle fracture mode than samples with serrated grain boundaries.
Samples with serrated grain boundaries will retain higher ductility than samples with straight grain boundaries.
The proposed morphology effect applies during significant mechanical loading in high-temperature-softening and low-temperature-embrittlement regimes.
The magnitude of the morphology effect may depend on loading rate, alloy composition, treatment parameters, and other microstructural details.
A comparison of identical-composition samples with confirmed serrated versus straight boundaries can test the proposed morphology mechanism.
No significant morphology-dependent difference in toughness, ductility, or failure mode would falsify the hypothesis.
